## Why This Matters

L01 gave you the map — the paradigms, the workflow, and the mathematics underneath. This
lesson hands you the **tools that do the work**: the few Python libraries every ML project
leans on, the cloud notebook you will run them in, and the one three-line pattern that trains
*any* model. By the end you will have trained and graded a real classifier — before the course
has taught you a single algorithm. That is deliberate: feel the workflow first, open the
algorithms later.

This lesson assumes you can already program in Python (your COMP 3082 background). We are not
teaching the language — we are teaching the **ML toolkit** built on top of it.

## The Scientific Python Stack

Machine learning in Python rests on four libraries, each with a clear job:

| Library | What it gives you | You use it to... |
|---------|-------------------|------------------|
| **NumPy** | the `ndarray` — fast numerical arrays and vectorized math | hold and crunch numbers; it is what pandas and scikit-learn store data in underneath |
| **pandas** | the `DataFrame` — a labeled table (rows = examples, columns = features) | load, clean, and select your data; a dataset *is* a `DataFrame` |
| **matplotlib** | plotting | look at the data before and after modeling (always plot first) |
| **scikit-learn** | the classic-ML algorithms behind one uniform API | split data, train models, score them |

You met the idea in L01 — a dataset is a matrix of rows and columns. pandas is how that matrix
becomes something you can load and slice; NumPy is the engine under it; scikit-learn is what
turns it into a model.

## The scikit-learn Estimator API

The reason scikit-learn is the backbone of this course is **consistency**: every model — a
nearest-neighbor classifier, linear regression, a support vector machine — is an *estimator*
that speaks the same three verbs.

```python
from sklearn.neighbors import KNeighborsClassifier

model = KNeighborsClassifier(n_neighbors=5)   # 1. choose a model
model.fit(X_train, y_train)                   # 2. fit:     learn from training data
predictions = model.predict(X_test)           # 3. predict: label new data
accuracy    = model.score(X_test, y_test)     #    score:   grade against known answers
```

::: {.callout-note}
**`fit` / `predict` / `score` is the whole interface.** Swap `KNeighborsClassifier` for
`LinearRegression` or `SVC` and these lines do not change. Learn the pattern once and every
later lesson reuses it — which is exactly why we can train a model today and *understand* it
later.
:::

One rule comes with the API and never leaves: **`fit` on the training data, `score` on the
held-out test data.** A model graded on the same examples it learned from is grading itself on
its own study sheet — the number flatters it. You will feel this directly in the lab, where a
hand-written rule that scores itself looks better than it is.

## The Runtime: Google Colab and the Setup Cell

The labs run in **Google Colab** — a free, in-browser Jupyter notebook with the scientific
stack preinstalled and no setup on your machine. Open the notebook from the **Colab badge** on
each concept page (the badge above opens this lesson's lab).

Colab **resets to a clean machine every time you open a notebook**, so each lab is
**self-contained**: it carries its own setup. That setup is deliberately **two cells**:

1. **An install-only cell** (`%pip install ...`) — run once.
2. **An imports + seed + data cell** — imports the libraries, fixes the random seed (so your
   numbers match everyone else's), and builds the data.

Splitting them means that when you re-run the imports while experimenting — which you will do
constantly — you do **not** re-trigger the install. Use `%pip` (not `!pip`): the `%` magic
installs into the *running* kernel.

::: {.callout-tip title="Why a fixed seed?"}
Every lab calls `np.random.default_rng(11)` before generating data. Seeding the random number
generator makes the synthetic data — and therefore every accuracy you compute — **identical
for everyone**, so your result and the expected output can be compared exactly.
:::

## Reproducible Local Environments with `uv`

Colab is the default, but you will sometimes want to run locally. The modern, fast way to get
a reproducible Python environment is [`uv`](https://docs.astral.sh/uv/) — a single tool that
manages the interpreter, a virtual environment, and your dependencies, pinned in a lockfile so
the project runs the same on any machine.

```bash
uv init coqui-lab          # create a project (pyproject.toml + a pinned environment)
uv add scikit-learn numpy pandas matplotlib   # add dependencies, locked
uv run jupyter lab         # run inside the project's environment
```

That is the local mirror of Colab's install cell: `uv add scikit-learn` does locally what
`%pip install scikit-learn` does in the notebook — the difference is that `uv` **locks** the
versions, so "works on my machine" becomes "works on every machine."

## FAQ / Industry Reality

**"Do I have to install anything to start?"** — No. Colab has the whole stack preinstalled;
the install cell is there to model the pattern (and to add anything Colab lacks). Local `uv`
is for when you want the project on your own machine.

**"pandas or NumPy — which do I reach for?"** — pandas for *tables* (loading, cleaning,
selecting columns), NumPy for *numbers* (arrays and math). In practice you use pandas to
prepare the data and hand the numeric part to scikit-learn, which works in NumPy underneath.

**"Is k-Nearest-Neighbors important?"** — Not as a topic here; we use it as a **black box** —
the simplest thing that has a `fit`/`predict`/`score` interface — so you can run the workflow
before any algorithm is taught. We never derive it; Unit II opens with models we *do* derive.

## Summary / Cheat-sheet

| Thing | The one-liner |
|-------|---------------|
| NumPy / pandas | numbers (`ndarray`) / labeled tables (`DataFrame`) |
| matplotlib | plot first, always |
| scikit-learn | models behind one API |
| The recipe | `model.fit(X_train, y_train)` · `model.predict(X)` · `model.score(X_test, y_test)` |
| Golden rule | fit on training data, score on held-out test data |
| Colab | preinstalled stack; resets on open, so labs carry a two-cell setup |
| `uv` | reproducible *local* environments (locked dependencies) |
